episodes: Ep 162: Ship 42 stays healthy in orbit after Booster 22 aborted its tower catch over a guidance issue.
Ep 161: SpaceX plans a $74 billion investment in supercomputing campuses to power its AI ambitions.
Ep 160: Zelensky reports Starshield speed limits resumed at 161 kilometers per hour for frontline troops.
Ep 159: SpaceX signed a turnkey heterojunction solar-cell line to scale Starmind satellite output past 100 GW.
Ep 157: Falcon 9 lifts a classified payload from Vandenberg tonight while new medium-lift vehicles near first flights.
Ep 156: Starship Flight 15 targets the first catch of both stages next week.
Ep 155: NASA reuses Curiosity rover parts for its PROMISE lunar south-pole mission, lowering risk for sustained outpost operations.
Ep 154: Musk's hint at a 500-ton Raptor 4 could unlock greater deep-space capability for Starship.
Ep 153: SpaceX targets the first upper-stage catch on Starship Flight 15 for November 13, advancing full rapid reuse of both stages.
Ep 152: Qualcomm Dragonwing platforms will power tens of thousands of Starlink Mobile 5G base stations starting in 2027.
Ep 151: Colossus 2 now leads global AI compute with 1.11 million H100 equivalents at its Memphis site.
Ep 150: Starlink terminals coordinated an Atlantic rescue in real time yesterday.
Ep 149: Musk revives TSMC Terafab talks and lifts SPCX in premarket trading.
Ep 148: Artemis III now locks Blue Origin’s lander in orbit first before NASA commits the SLS crew launch.
Ep 147: SpaceX completed three static fires in three days while rehearsing ship catches at Starbase.
Ep 146: The FCC's vote to open 482 MHz of spectrum expands Starlink Mobile's path to compete with terrestrial carriers on direct-to-phone service.
Ep 145: Crew Dragon Grace docked with the ISS after seven hours and fifty-five minutes, the fastest US crewed flight to the station.
Ep 144: SpaceX plans 10,000 annual Starship launches from Louisiana site alone.
Ep 143: Raptor 4 targets 300 tons of sea-level thrust at Raptor 3 mass, pushing Super Heavy toward 9,900 tons total.
Ep 142: SpaceX fired all 33 Raptor engines on the Super Heavy booster for a full-duration static fire, clearing the immediate next step for Starship Flight 15.
Ep 141: NASA's updated refueling outlook for Starship HLS trims Artemis launch needs from 22 to roughly 6-8.
Ep 140: NASA’s first public Starship cabin images advance dual 2028 lunar landing options.
Ep 139: Next LC-36A tower module addition moves Florida Starship operations closer to first flights.
Ep 138: SpaceX lofted Turkey’s first homegrown satellite while an xAI data-center lawsuit advanced in court.
Ep 137: SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship upper stage on Flight 15.
Ep 136: Falcon 9 booster B1063 reaches its 36th flight today, extending the record for reusable first stages.
Ep 135: Analysts expect SpaceX to post its first profitable quarter since the IPO when earnings land Tuesday.
Ep 134: Ukraine negotiates directly with SpaceX and the Pentagon to lift Starshield speed caps on drones.
Ep 133: SpaceX Dragon experiments on artificial retinas and brain tissue now run in sustained microgravity aboard the station.
Ep 132: SpaceX thrusters give the Tesla Roadster aerial flight and roll capability ahead of 2028 production.
Ep 131: SpaceX is guaranteeing to cover any Grok Bot purchase errors to encourage wider use of the AI assistant for shopping.
Ep 130: Ukraine drone missions lost satellite links above 100 mph after SpaceX added an overnight Starshield speed limit.
Ep 129: Booster 23's rollout to Massey for cryo testing keeps the next Starship hardware cycle on schedule.
Ep 128: A single Starlink satellite held its orbit to within 44 meters for three months while fighting atmospheric drag at 460 km.
Ep 126: Orbital tests of laser power beaming and radiation-hardened AI chips move data-center concepts into space.
Ep 124: SpaceX reports Starship pad construction at Kennedy Space Center nearly complete with acceptance testing now underway.
Ep 123: SpaceX is lining up forty billion dollars to buy Nvidia chips, underscoring the scale of its AI infrastructure buildout.
Ep 122: Dragon now owns every U.S. record for fastest trips to the ISS after Crew-13 docked in seven hours fifty-five minutes.
Ep 121: SpaceX is renaming its AI unit to SpaceXSI while scrubbing an SDA satellite launch and prepping Starship Ship 43 for a possible Florida debut.
Ep 120: Starship's orbital debut placed twenty-six Starlink V3 satellites each adding roughly ten times the capacity of a Falcon 9 launch.
Ep 119: Falcon Heavy side boosters separated at two minutes twenty seven seconds on NROL-97.
Ep 118: SpaceX flew three rockets in a single day, placing astronauts on the ISS, a Google AI test satellite in orbit, and a classified NRO payload.
Ep 117: Two Indian startups will test orbital computing and thermal sensing on a Falcon 9 tonight.
Ep 115: Starlink secured an internet provider license in Bosnia and Herzegovina, opening service rollout in the coming weeks.
Ep 114: TakeMe2Space will fly an orbital AI computer on a Falcon 9 in three days.
Ep 113: Starship will attempt its first sustained orbit on Monday after 13 suborbital flights that kept the upper stage on passively safe paths.
Ep 112: Four Starshield launches in 43 days from one pad show how quickly the Space Force is scaling its classified constellation.
Ep 111: Google's first orbital AI satellite will test whether chips can shed heat in vacuum aboard a SpaceX launch next week.
Ep 110: SpaceX gains classified Pentagon tracking data to sharpen collision avoidance for its eleven thousand satellites.
Ep 109: SpaceX annexes seven thousand acres at Starbase to expand Starship production capacity.
Ep 108: Raptor engines on parade in McGregor spotlight the production scale behind Starship's orbital target.
Ep 107: SpaceX is preparing a single-price global Starlink Mobile service that could extend direct-to-cell coverage to new regions without regional pricing tiers.
Ep 106: SpaceX's FCC filing for an orbital data center constellation brings re-entry debris and collision risks under formal regulatory review for the first time.
Ep 105: Starlink’s secondary network architecture opens a new path for direct device connectivity without relying solely on terrestrial gateways.
Ep 104: NASA plans to keep Starliner in service longer shift Dragon's retirement target to 2030 and change how crews reach the station.
Ep 103: A single Falcon 9 booster completing its 13th flight for a classified payload shows how reuse directly expands national-security launch capacity.
Ep 102: Closing new Falcon 9 reservations shows the booster fleet has reached its sustainable reuse limit and is now fully allocated.
Ep 101: Rocket Lab's Neutron development at Wallops Island introduces the first credible pressure on Falcon 9 dominance in the medium-lift segment.
Ep 100: SpaceX completes the O3b mPOWER constellation with a Cape Canaveral launch while preparing a Vandenberg mission for USSF-259.
Ep 99: Roadster October 1 demo date puts SpaceX thruster hover tech on public display for the first time.
Ep 98: Starship reuse cost drops open orbital AI compute as an alternative to land-based data centers.
Ep 97: SpaceX's $1.11 billion monthly AI hosting deal ties orbital launch capacity directly to terrestrial compute expansion.
Ep 96: Booster 22's rollout to Massey's for paired testing directly advances the hardware validation sequence needed for Flight 15.
Ep 95: SpaceX’s first Louisiana job posting marks the concrete start of a second Gulf Coast launch site that could raise East Coast flight rate.
Ep 94: New FAA-approved Pacific contingency zones give Starship test flights wider safe-return options while leaving Vandenberg operations untouched.
Ep 93: Musk's Raptor V3 simplifications and xAI's new power-plant plans both target the same bottleneck: scaling reliable hardware and power for orbital compute.
Ep 92: Split manufacturing for Starship separates booster and upper-stage lines to cut serial bottlenecks in final assembly.
Ep 91: Starship V3 upper-stage changes at Pad 2 expose the exact hardware limits that must be solved before the first orbital flight can succeed.
Ep 90: xAI's Memphis data center outage reveals how single-site power and cooling limits now constrain Grok-scale inference.
Ep 89: FAA clearance for a wider Starship flight corridor moves the program closer to routine orbital refueling demonstrations.
Ep 88: Falcon 9's new reuse record tightens the cost curve that makes frequent orbital missions routine.
Ep 87: SpaceX’s $220 million water infrastructure pledge in Brownsville secures additional land that directly supports higher Starship launch cadence at Starbase.
Ep 86: A propulsion leak in the Crew Dragon forces NASA and SpaceX to postpone the next crewed ISS mission, tightening the safety margin on an aging spacecraft design.
Ep 85: A Crew-13 date shift shows how Dragon mission timelines stay tightly coupled to ISS crew rotation needs.
Ep 84: Starbase growth is now forcing Texas road upgrades that directly shape how quickly the site can scale launch cadence.
Ep 83: Spectrum rules at the FCC now sit at the center of how quickly competing satellite networks can scale.
Ep 82: Cursor's deployment inside victim networks by ransomware groups shows how widely the AI coding tool has spread through the Musk stack.
Ep 81: SpaceX's planned $100 billion Louisiana Starbase would support thousands of annual Starship launches from a new Gulf Coast hub.
Ep 80: Louisiana launch pad plans would give Starship a new Gulf Coast site that directly raises the achievable flight rate.
Ep 79: Proprietary alloys and a dedicated gas trader for Texas facilities show SpaceX tightening control over Starship materials and energy inputs.
Ep 78: Forecasts for more than 6,500 new Earth observation satellites by 2035 highlight why rapid reusable launch capacity will determine who captures the coming manufacturing surge.
Ep 77: Trump's new space transportation policy could open federal land for heavy-lift spaceports, directly expanding the sites available for Starship and Falcon operations.
Ep 76: Recovering Ship 40 after weeks at sea will show how much structural and thermal data survives saltwater exposure for the next round of Starship iterations.
Ep 75: Regulatory steps in South Africa and India move Starlink closer to new markets while Louisiana site talks advance launch options.
Ep 74: Falcon Heavy’s selection for the 2028 Dragonfly mission shows how heavy-lift capacity directly enables long-duration outer-planet rotorcraft flights.
Ep 73: Recovering Starship Ship 40 after 24 days at sea supplies the first long-duration ocean-exposure data for upper-stage reuse planning.
Ep 72: Starbase expansion plans in south Texas would add launch pads and production space that directly raise the ceiling on Starship flight rate.
Ep 71: Falcon 9's 38-minute coast-to-coast cadence shows how rapid booster recovery and parallel pad processing are lifting annual flight-rate ceilings.
Ep 70: Starship still lacks an orbital refueling demo after thirteen flights, keeping the revised 2028 Mars cargo window dependent on solving that single bottleneck first.
Ep 69: Plans for a new Starship static-fire site in Florida move the upper-stage catch test campaign closer to dual-coast operations.
Ep 68: Starship 14's planned tower catch tests the lighter booster's recovery hardware and moves rapid reuse one flight closer.
Ep 67: Starship's push toward 100-ton lunar deliveries reframes the hardware requirements for routine Moon cargo runs.
Ep 66: Tuesday's rescheduled Starlink launch from Cape Canaveral keeps the year's 72nd broadband mission on track after the Monday scrub.
Ep 65: Experts labeling Starship’s heat shield a potential dead end could push the next full orbital refueling attempt back by months.
Ep 64: West Coast launch cadence reaching its 50th flight this year shows how Vandenberg infrastructure is sustaining overall flight rate while East Coast pads slow.
Ep 63: Rough seas in the Indian Ocean now threaten to end recovery of the Ship from Flight 13 before it reaches port.
Ep 62: Monday's Starlink launch from Cape Canaveral resumes constellation expansion and tests direct-to-cell backhaul at scale.
Ep 61: NROL-95's launch and Redwire's Starfall agreement show how national-security and microgravity hardware are scaling on the same Falcon and Dragon platforms.
Ep 60: Confirmation of a Falcon 9 stage striking the moon tests deep-space tracking networks while exposing gaps in lunar debris protocols ahead of crewed missions.
Ep 59: SpaceX Q2 2026 Earnings Special: Revenue reached $7.814 billion, up 92 percent from a year earlier, in the company's first earnings report as a public company.
Ep 58: NASA needing a heavier vehicle for ISS deorbit highlights why current Falcon-class lift falls short for large end-of-life missions.
Ep 57: Starship Flight 14's first orbital attempt this month now depends on whether the upper-stage heat shield and booster catch systems both clear their final checks.
Ep 56: Starlink's launch priority is forcing satellite operators to secure alternative vehicles or delay deployments.
Ep 55: A defunct Falcon 9 stage impact on the Moon gives astronomers a calibrated data point on crater formation from a known mass and velocity.
Ep 54: Starlink satellites captured Starship in orbit, giving engineers direct visual data on upper-stage behavior after deployment.
Ep 53: Starlink V3 satellites imaging Starship V3 in orbit tightens the feedback loop between constellation hardware and next-block vehicle development.
Ep 52: No fresh SpaceX hardware or mission updates appear in today's reporting, so the focus stays on steady progress across reuse and refueling goals.
Ep 51: Raptor 3’s static-fire campaign on the V3 ascent configuration narrows the thrust-to-weight gap that still separates Starship from full rapid reuse.
Ep 50: Flight 13’s Ship 40 splashdown and V3 satellite checkout move the first orbital tower catch one flight closer.
Ep 49: A fresh $1.6 billion Pentagon award secures 18 Falcon 9 missions through 2027 and extends national-security launch cadence from Vandenberg.
Ep 48: Ship 40’s continued float after Flight 13 gives SpaceX its first long-duration data set on an intact upper-stage thermal-protection system in seawater.
Ep 47: Heat-shield performance on the Ship upper stage during Flight 13 now clears a key thermal margin for repeated orbital reentries.
Ep 46: Starship Flight 13's intentional faster ascent supplied new heat-shield performance data that narrows the remaining steps to a Super Heavy booster tower catch on Flight 14.
Ep 45: Starship Flight 13's intact upper-stage splashdown moves the program one step closer to attempting the first tower catch of the Ship on Flight 14.
Ep 44: Starship Flight 13's V3 Starlink deployment and intact splashdown clears the path for a tower-catch attempt on the next flight.
Ep 43: Tropical Storm Bertha forces Starship Flight 13 to Friday, extending the test campaign's weather-driven pauses at Starbase.
Ep 42: Starship Flight 13 tonight will test Starlink deployment from the full stack for the first time, advancing orbital refueling hardware validation.

Ep 41: Northrop Grumman’s MRV-1 servicer is now on orbit after its Falcon 9 ride, beginning the first on-orbit installation of propulsion pods that could extend the life of three aging commercial satellites.
Ep 40: Northrop Grumman’s robot-armed satellite heads to orbit today on a Falcon 9, moving on-orbit servicing from study to flight hardware.
Ep 39: Vandenberg’s 50th launch of 2026 shows Falcon 9 reuse sustaining cadence while Starship readies its next V3 test flight.
Ep 38: Starship’s July 23 target now includes the first V3 satellites, determining whether the vehicle can deliver operational gigabit links before year-end.
Ep 37: Infrastructure moves in Texas and Louisiana plus Falcon’s 50th California flight of the year point to concrete steps toward higher launch cadence while Starship testing continues.
Ep 36: Raptor ignition gaps on the latest Starship test force two engine swaps and reset the timeline for proving rapid booster reuse.
Ep 35: Raptor ignition failure on Flight 13 forces a rapid re-test cycle that tests how quickly Starbase can iterate on engine-start reliability.
Ep 34: Closing the Flight 12 mishap probe removes the last regulatory hold on Starship's engine-relight demonstration that directly gates Artemis III lander timelines.
Ep 33: Starship Flight 13’s planned debut of V3 satellites will test whether the vehicle can deliver operational payloads while advancing rapid-reuse goals.
Ep 32: B1080’s 28th flight targets the 600th Falcon booster reuse, further compressing the marginal cost of each kilogram to orbit.
Ep 31: Flight 13's propellant and avionics upgrades move Starship one step closer to demonstrating the rapid reuse that would collapse launch costs.

Ep 30: Starship's July 16 flight will attempt the first orbital deployment of Starlink V3 satellites, directly testing the upgraded laser links and mass capacity needed for the next phase of constellation growth.
Ep 29: Booster 20’s record-duration static fire moves Starship Flight 13 to a July 15 target and tests the thermal margins needed for rapid booster reuse.
Ep 28: Booster 20's rollout to Pad 2 and the 420-ton crane installation at Cape Gigabay mark concrete steps toward higher Starship flight cadence and ground operations.
Ep 27: Falcon 9’s 36th flight today extends booster life limits and sustains the cadence needed for Starlink’s record deployment year.
Ep 26: Starship lunar ride-share contracts move orbital refueling and heavy-payload delivery timelines forward by demonstrating early commercial demand.
Ep 25: Record Falcon cadence and a fresh rideshare deployment show how reuse margins are widening the gap between annual launch capacity and demand.
Ep 24: Falcon 9's Starlink flight doubles as a chip-test platform, probing semiconductor behavior under launch loads.
Ep 23: Ship 40’s completed static fire and a semiconductor test bed riding today’s Falcon 9 both test hardware that must survive repeated thermal and vibration loads before scaling.
Ep 22: Starship engine tests clear a key hurdle on the road to the thirteenth flight and the first orbital refueling demonstration.
Ep 21: Starship’s six-engine static fire advances the thirteenth flight-test campaign by validating the full Raptor cluster ahead of orbital attempts.
Ep 20: The 1,000th Merlin 1D engine marks how Falcon reuse has turned repeated flights into the main driver of engine reliability gains.
Ep 19: An eight-mile gas pipeline at Starbase targets the propellant bottleneck that has limited Starship launch cadence.
Ep 18: Measured dry-mass cuts on IFT-12 hardware widen the payload margin that orbital refueling must close before Mars missions become routine.
Ep 17: A 15,000-pound SiriusXM satellite launch on Falcon 9 demonstrates the vehicle's sustained heavy-payload cadence while Starship 40's static fire keeps Flight 13 hardware moving forward.
Ep 16: Ship 40’s single-engine static fire clears the first hot-fire gate for the vehicle that will fly Starship’s next integrated test.
Ep 15: Starpipe's dedicated Texas gas line removes a propellant-delivery bottleneck that has capped Starship launch cadence at Starbase.
Ep 14: Vandenberg’s cleared expansion and yesterday’s Starlink launch raise Falcon reuse counts while Starship hardware moves toward orbital compute tests.
Ep 13: Vandenberg site clearance and a Texas court ruling together remove two long-standing constraints on West Coast and Texas launch rates.
Ep 11: A 2022 geomagnetic storm that destroyed 40 Starlink satellites is now informing how the constellation hardens against atmospheric drag as launch rates climb.
Ep 10: The week's biggest developments, pulled together — what actually moved, why it matters, and what to watch next.
Ep 9: Mechazilla upgrades at Starbase tighten the turnaround loop that must close before Starship can attempt its first tower catch.
Ep 8: Falcon 9's classified NRO launch from Vandenberg shows how booster reuse now supports steady cadence on sensitive national-security missions.
Ep 7: Raptor 3 engine shutdowns during boostback keep Starship reuse timelines uncertain even after the redesign.
Ep 6: Five uncrewed Starships aimed at the 2026 Mars window will test whether orbital refueling can deliver the propellant margins needed for crewed flights inside five years.
Ep 5: Shotwell’s one-Starship-per-month target now depends on whether the new Florida pads can support the same rapid propellant loading and booster turnaround already proven at Starbase.
Ep 4: Falcon 9's first flight after the Nasdaq debut tests whether public markets alter the company's launch tempo at all.
Ep 3: The week's biggest developments, pulled together — what actually moved, why it matters, and what to watch next.
